newsitem.title: USA: Deadline passes with no strike in Ford-UAW talks.
newsitem.headline: Deadline passes with no strike in Ford-UAW talks.

text.p: Disagreements over outsourcing pushed labor contract talks at Ford Motor Co. into the early morning hours Sunday, but the United Auto Workers told members not to strike the automaker's plants.
The union did not formally extend the automaker's past three-year contract, which expired at midnight Saturday.
"They told us to keep people working, but there's been no formal extension," said Jerry Klein, president of UAW Local 249 in Kansas City, Mo. "We're just sitting in the prairie waiting."

Ford spokesman Jon Harmon said at about 2:15 a.m. EDT that an agreement was not expected until sometime later Sunday, but added that Ford plants were operating normally. "There's no reason to expect production in any faciliity that has been scheduled will be disrupted," he told reporters.
UAW President Stephen Yokich, taking a break from bargaining shortly after midnight, refused to talk to reporters at Ford World Headquarters here.
In a statement, Ford said talks were "continuing actively between the negotiating teams."
"Important issues remain unresolved, but the tone of the discussions remains constructive," the automaker said.

Ford and UAW negotiators had met non-stop since 8 a.m. Saturday in a drive to reach a new national labor contract covering the automaker's approximately 105,000 UAW hourly workers. The UAW is expected to try to use the pact as a pattern for General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp., which employ 216,000 and 66,000 UAW workers, respectively.
Klein and other local union leaders at Ford plants said negotiators were having difficulty reaching agreement on issues related to outsourcing.

The UAW wants the right to strike when it disagrees with the company's decisions to transfer work to outside suppliers, which would give it greater leverage to preserve jobs. The union also has sought guaranteed employment levels that would require the companies to replace more retiring workers.
Earlier Saturday, Ford officials said they were optimistic that a pact could be reached without a work stoppage.
In the last UAW contract negotiations in 1993, also led by Ford, it took a marathon 40-hour bargaining session that lasted nearly 24 hours past the deadline to produce a settlement.
Negotiations between the UAW and the Big Three have run past the contract expiration deadline in each of the past three pacts -- 1987, 1990 and 1993.
The UAW Friday extended its contracts with GM and Chrysler, pledging not to strike those automakers while it continues bargaining with Ford.
